text: Object storage has become the default substrate for machine learning teams because it scales horizontally, decouples compute from data, and lets many training jobs read the same corpus concurrently without a central file server becoming a bottleneck.

Preparing a pretraining corpus is mostly a data-engineering problem. Raw web crawls are noisy, duplicated, and full of boilerplate, so a curation pipeline that deduplicates, filters, and redacts is often worth more than another few billion unfiltered tokens.

Exact deduplication removes documents that are byte-for-byte identical after normalization. It is cheap, runs on CPU, and typically strips a surprising fraction of a crawl because navigation pages and syndicated articles repeat across many domains.

Heuristic quality filters score each document on simple signals: word count, mean word length, the ratio of symbols to words, the fraction of non-alphanumeric characters, and how many lines repeat. Documents that fail the thresholds are dropped before training ever sees them.

Versioning every stage of a curation pipeline as its own sharded dataset gives you an audit trail. If a downstream model behaves oddly you can diff the deduplicated corpus against the filtered one and see exactly which documents each stage removed.

Sharding a corpus into many part files lets a distributed data loader assign shards to workers without coordination. Each worker streams its shards directly from object storage, so throughput scales with the number of readers rather than the size of any single file.

PII redaction protects both the people whose data was scraped and the team training the model. A named-entity recognizer finds emails, phone numbers, names, and identifiers, and a modifier replaces, masks, or hashes each span so the cleaned text can be shared more freely.

Tokenization turns raw text into the integer sequences a model actually consumes. Byte-pair encoding and unigram models both aim to balance vocabulary size against sequence length, and the choice interacts with how much multilingual or code data sits in the corpus.

A lineage manifest records how many documents entered and left each stage, plus the bytes written. That lets a platform team reason about write amplification: raw plus deduplicated plus filtered plus redacted can be several copies of the corpus living in storage at once.

Retrieval-augmented generation shifts some of the burden from parameters to an external index, but the index still has to be built from a clean corpus. Garbage documents retrieved at inference time degrade answers just as surely as garbage tokens seen during pretraining.

Fine-tuning a base model on a narrow, high-quality corpus often beats training a larger model on a noisier one. Curation is how you buy quality: it is far cheaper to filter aggressively than to pay for the compute to memorize boilerplate and duplicated text.

Data loaders for large corpora usually stream from object storage rather than staging everything on local disk. Presigned URLs let a training node fetch a shard directly and securely, which keeps the storage layer stateless and easy to scale out across a cluster.

Reproducibility in machine learning starts with the data. If you cannot point at the exact set of shards a checkpoint was trained on, you cannot rerun the experiment, and subtle corpus changes between runs become impossible to distinguish from changes to the model.

Symbol-heavy documents such as tables of stock tickers or dumps of configuration often carry little natural-language signal for a language model. A symbol-to-word ratio filter is a blunt but effective way to remove them without hand-labeling every page.

Content-defined chunking and near-duplicate detection catch documents that are almost but not quite identical, like the same article with a different header. Exact deduplication is the fast first pass; fuzzy deduplication on a GPU cluster handles the rest when budget allows.

Storing curated corpora in a single object-storage bucket with a clear key prefix per project keeps costs legible. A finance team can attribute spend by prefix, and an engineer can list exactly which stage outputs exist for any given curation run.

Evaluation sets must be held out from the training corpus, and deduplication is how you enforce that. If an evaluation document leaks into pretraining through a duplicate, your reported metrics overstate how well the model generalizes to genuinely unseen text.

A good curation pipeline is idempotent and restartable. Because each stage writes its own immutable, versioned output, a failure part way through only costs the stages that had not yet completed, and rerunning cannot corrupt the shards that already landed.

Multilingual corpora need language identification before filtering, because thresholds tuned for English mislabel perfectly good text in other scripts. Running a fast classifier first lets each language use its own quality thresholds rather than a single global rule.

Versioning every stage of a curation pipeline as its own sharded dataset gives you an audit trail. If a downstream model behaves oddly you can diff the deduplicated corpus against the filtered one and see exactly which documents each stage removed.

Repeated-line filters catch documents where the same sentence appears over and over, a common artifact of scraped forums and auto-generated pages. Such repetition teaches a model almost nothing yet consumes context length and training compute.

The cost of storing intermediate curation stages is usually dwarfed by the cost of the training run itself, which is why keeping every stage is a sensible default. Storage is cheap insurance against having to re-curate a multi-terabyte crawl from scratch.

Streaming curation lets you process a corpus larger than memory by loading one shard at a time, transforming it, and writing the result before moving on. The peak memory footprint stays bounded no matter how large the overall dataset grows.

A quality preset is just a named bundle of thresholds. A lenient preset keeps almost everything for exploratory work; a strict preset aggressively prunes for a final production corpus. Exposing presets keeps the common cases one click away without hiding the knobs.

Curation and privacy overlap wherever scraped data contains personal information. Redacting emails, phone numbers, and government identifiers before the corpus is stored reduces the blast radius if the bucket is ever misconfigured or a shard is shared too widely.

A curation run's manifest is small enough to fetch on every dashboard load, so aggregating stats across dozens of runs stays fast even when the underlying shards total many gigabytes in the bucket.

Because the pipeline writes plain JSON Lines, any downstream tool can consume a stage's output without a special reader. A data scientist can open a shard in a notebook, and a training job can stream it, from the exact same objects in storage.

Exact deduplication is deterministic, which matters for reproducibility: given the same input shards the same documents are always removed, so two engineers curating the same crawl independently arrive at byte-identical deduplicated output.

The write-amplification story is the point where storage economics meets machine learning. Keeping raw, deduplicated, filtered, and redacted copies is deliberate: each supports a different question, from debugging a filter to auditing what personal data was removed.

A demo corpus should be small enough to curate in seconds yet varied enough to exercise every stage. Bundling duplicates, low-quality pages, and synthetic personal data means a first run visibly removes and redacts documents without any external download.

Handing a training job a stable, versioned corpus prefix in object storage decouples the two teams. The data team iterates on curation and publishes new versions, while the modeling team pins the exact version they trained against for full reproducibility.
